subtype: Cheering and chanting at school events [Expressing]
passage:
Sports day at the school ground, and Blue House was winning the relay. Yusuf stood on the bench with his whole row, clapping in time: clap-clap, stamp, "BLUE, BLUE, NEVER THROUGH!" His voice was already hoarse and his chest felt huge.
Then Deepak from Yellow House tripped on the last bend and fell flat. A few Blue boys started a new chant: "Yellow jelly, jelly legs!" It caught fast. Deepak got up slowly, his knee bleeding, and did not look at the stands.
Yusuf's clapping stopped. The chant felt different in his mouth now.
He jumped down, cupped his hands and shouted the loudest thing he could: "Come on, Deepak, finish it!" Two boys beside him joined in. Deepak limped over the line, and the P.T. teacher ran to check his knee.

qa.q: What did the Blue House row chant while clapping?
qa.a: "BLUE, BLUE, NEVER THROUGH!"

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling before and after Deepak fell?
qa.a: Before the fall Yusuf felt excited and proud, with a hoarse voice and a huge chest; after the mocking chant began, the stopped clapping suggests he felt uneasy, maybe ashamed to be part of it.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that other children in a crowd could copy?
qa.a: He stopped joining the mocking chant and started a cheer for the fallen runner instead, which turned the crowd's energy back to support.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt hearing both chants?
qa.a: The jelly-legs chant probably made him feel humiliated while he was already hurt, and the cheer for him to finish may have helped him keep going.

grounding: At a school sports event, cheering brings excitement and unity until it turns into mockery, and a child shows where cheering should end.

At the inter-school cricket match, I sat two rows behind Asif. He was the one who started the rhythm: bang the plastic bottles twice, clap once, shout our school's name. Soon the whole stand was doing it, and Asif was grinning so wide you could see his missing tooth.
Then the other team's fielder dropped an easy catch. The big boys behind us yelled, "Butterfingers! Go home!" and started banging the bottles for that instead.
Asif turned and looked at them. He put his bottle down between his feet and sat back down. He didn't clap again until our batsman hit a four.
I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Maybe he felt sorry for the fielder. Maybe he just didn't like the big boys taking over his beat.
- Sumit

qa.q: What rhythm did Asif start in the stand?
qa.a: Bang the plastic bottles twice, clap once, shout the school's name.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he put his bottle down?
qa.a: He may have felt uncomfortable or sorry for the fielder being mocked; he might also have felt annoyed that the big boys took over his beat, and Sumit cannot tell which.

qa.q: What could Sumit try next time the stand turns mocking?
qa.a: Sumit could stop joining in too, and restart the school cheer so the noise goes back to supporting their own team.

qa.q: How might the fielder who dropped the catch feel hearing the stand?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and low, since an ordinary mistake became a reason for a whole crowd to shout at him.

grounding: An observer watches a child lead group cheering at a match and then step back when the crowd turns to mocking the other side.

Second Saturday: In the second half the crowd began a new song about the other team's goalkeeper being fat. Lalremsiami sang it too, laughing, until the goalkeeper turned and she saw his face. He looked straight at their stand. She shut her mouth and held her scarf in both fists.
Third Saturday: Before the match she told Vishal, "I'll shout for our team, but not that song." Vishal thought, then nodded. "Make up a better one." She did, all about their striker's fast feet, and three kids near them joined in.

qa.a: She told Vishal where she would stop and made up a new chant for their own striker, which kept the fun of cheering without the mockery.

qa.a: Vishal seems to respect it, and challenging her to make a better chant shows he accepts cheering can stay fun without hurting anyone.

Monday: Ayesha came home and put her hair in a tight bun, just like Damini Ma'am's. She practised writing her capital A with the same curly tail. "Ma'am says my handwriting is improving," she told Ammi, glowing.
Wednesday: In maths, Ma'am wrote a sum on the board, and it was wrong. Ravi said so. Ma'am's cheeks went pink. Ayesha stared at her book. She felt oddly let down, as if a wall had cracked.

Nikita wanted everything like her big sister Shreya: the same high ponytail, the same way of hooking her thumbs in her pockets, the same roller skates one day. Today Shreya had a skating practice across town, and Nikita begged to come.

When I got jaundice in Class 5 and missed three weeks of school, I thought I'd fail everything. Then every Friday, Maria came to our gate with a plastic folder. She had copied all the notes by hand for me, in blue ink with red headings, even the diagrams.
I just said "thanks" the first time. Then Mummy showed me the date at the top of one page: Maria had written it at eleven at night.
When I went back to school, I didn't know how to say thank you properly. So I spent Sunday teaching her how to bowl a leg-spinner, which she'd been begging me about for months. She got it on the fifteenth try and screamed.
Now she bowls better than me.
- Lalit

qa.a: Red headings.

qa.a: Lalit probably felt surprised and moved, realising Maria had stayed up until eleven at night to copy the notes.

qa.q: How might Maria see the bowling lesson?
qa.a: Maria likely felt delighted and thanked in return, seeing Lalit give time to help her with something she cared about.

Coach's note, Tuesday, junior cricket camp
This morning Deepak arrived early and saw Lakshmi Amma, our groundskeeper, watering the pitch with a heavy pipe before sunrise. He asked her why. She told him the pitch cracks if it isn't watered twice a day.
After practice, Deepak stayed back. He picked up stray balls, rolled them into the basket, and then went up to Lakshmi Amma. He said, "Thank you for our pitch. I didn't know you come so early." She looked surprised, then smiled.

The school bus was packed and steamy because of the rain, and the driver had the radio on loud. When they got off at the gate, Keerthana stepped in a puddle and slid, landing on her bottom with a splash.
Everyone near the gate shouted with laughter. Arnab froze. Was she hurt? Was this bad?
Then he saw Keerthana was laughing hardest of all, flicking mud at her friends. "I'm a mud buffalo!" she yelled. Arnab laughed too.
But a boy kept doing an exaggerated slip, again and again, calling "Mud girl! Mud girl!" Keerthana's grin went stiff. She stood up and wiped her hands on her skirt without looking at anyone.
Arnab stopped laughing. He walked over and held out his handkerchief. "Want this?" She took it and nodded.

qa.q: What did Keerthana call herself after falling?
qa.a: A mud buffalo.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling at first, and how did Arnab tell that it changed?
qa.a: At first Keerthana was laughing hardest and joking, which showed she felt amused and included; when the boy kept mocking, her grin went stiff and she didn't look at anyone, which suggests she felt hurt and embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Arnab do when he noticed the change?
qa.a: He stopped laughing and offered his handkerchief, a small way of standing with her instead of laughing at her.

qa.q: If you were the boy mimicking the slip, what would you want to notice next time?
qa.a: You would want to watch whether the person is still laughing too; once their smile goes stiff, the joke is at them, not with them.

grounding: In the rain at the school gate, a child learns to tell shared laughter from mocking laughter by watching the other person.

"Jasleen, you laughed today when I said 'pee-zza' in English class."
"Everyone laughed, Devika. It was funny, na? I thought you were joking!"
"I wasn't. That's how my Dadi says it."

"That was different. We were both laughing. Today it was everyone laughing at me."

Devika shrugged. "Look if the person is laughing with their eyes, not just their mouth. Or just ask."
Jasleen nodded. "I'm sorry. Next time I'll ask."
"Okay." Devika smiled, and this time it reached her eyes.

Counsellor's note, Monday
Farhan's Dadi died last week. Today he cried in Hindi class when the teacher read a story about a grandmother. He asked me three times, "Will Dadi's bed stay in our house?" I told him each time, gently, that his family would decide, and that Dadi had died and would not come back.
At break he played cricket and shouted and laughed with his friends as usual. After break he sat alone on the steps and didn't want to go back to class.
I stayed with him and kept his routine as normal as I could: same lunch, same seat. I phoned his mother after school so we could share what we are both seeing and plan the week together.
- Ms Anjali, school counsellor

qa.q: What did Farhan ask the counsellor three times?
qa.a: "Will Dadi's bed stay in our house?"

qa.q: What might Farhan's switch from laughing at cricket to sitting alone show about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It shows grief coming in bursts: he could enjoy play for a while, then feel sad and heavy again and want to be alone.

qa.q: What steps did Ms Anjali take that protect Farhan?
qa.a: She answered his questions honestly each time, kept his routine steady, stayed with him, and spoke to his mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Farhan's classmates see his sudden change after break?
qa.a: They might be confused, since he was laughing at cricket, not knowing that grief can come and go like this.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a grieving child crying, asking repeated questions, playing, and withdrawing, and the adult keeping routine and giving honest answers.

Nani died on Sunday. Today I played ludo with my cousin Mehak and we laughed so much about her cheating. Then I saw Nani's glasses on the shelf and I stopped laughing. I felt bad for laughing at all.
I asked Mummy again tonight, "Is Nani really never coming back?" I know the answer. I just keep asking.

In the Himachal village, Omkar's Dadaji had died three days ago. The house was full of relatives and whispers, and nobody cooked the usual rajma.
Omkar kept going to the goat shed. He fed the goats, then sat and cried. Then he chased the kid goat around, laughing.
Later he asked his mother, "Where is Dadaji now?" She hugged him. "Dadaji's body has stopped, and he won't come back. But you can remember him with the goats."
Next morning, Dolma from next door came with a basket, as she always did. "Feed them with me?"
They fed the goats together. Omkar didn't talk much, but he did it every morning after that.

Keerthana had been Pranav's best friend since Class 1. Last week her family moved to Chennai, and since then the flat above had been silent.
At dinner in their Bengaluru flat, Pranav pushed the rice around the plate. For three mornings he had said his stomach hurt and asked to stay home.
His father sat down beside him instead of telling him to eat. "It's Keerthana, isn't it?"
Pranav's eyes filled. "Nobody saves my seat on the bus now. I sit alone."
His father didn't say "you'll make new friends." He just said, "That sounds lonely," and waited.
Pranav talked for a long time, about the bus, their secret knock on the ceiling, the stickers she left.
Only later did his father ask, "Should we write her a letter this weekend?"

qa.q: What did Keerthana and Pranav have on the ceiling?

qa.a: He listened first, named the lonely feeling, and waited before suggesting any fix, which let Pranav pour out what hurt.

qa.a: Pranav might have felt his pain was brushed aside as small, and he may have kept the hurt to himself.

grounding: A child who loses a best friend to a move feels deep hurt, and a parent listens before offering a fix.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage:
Ramesh wasn't picked for the school cricket team, and he had a maths exam tomorrow. At home, the TV was loud, his little cousins were running around, and there was nowhere quiet.
He went up to the terrace. His eyes stung, and he let a few tears come. Then he breathed in slowly, counting to four, and out to six, like Dilnaz Aunty had taught him.
He felt a little calmer, but still sad.
He went next door. Dilnaz Aunty, who helped him with maths, opened the door. "Ramesh? What's wrong?"
"I didn't make the team," he said, voice shaky.
She let him sit and listened, then said, "That's hard. Let's do ten minutes of maths, then we can talk more."

qa.q: Where did Ramesh go to cry?
qa.a: Up to the terrace.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when his eyes stung?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed about not being picked for the team, and stressed about the exam.

qa.q: What small steps helped Ramesh manage his sadness?
qa.a: He cried privately, breathed slowly, and then chose to tell a trusted adult, Dilnaz Aunty.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz Aunty feel when Ramesh came to her?
qa.a: She probably felt caring and glad he trusted her enough to share his hurt.

grounding: Under exam pressure, a child regulates sadness by crying privately, breathing slowly, and telling a trusted adult.

passage:
"Tenzin, helmet on."
"No!" Tenzin crossed his arms. "I'm not wearing that baby helmet!"
Tanuja, his mother, crouched down. "Why not?"
"The boys laugh. It's pink with bunnies."
"Ah." She paused. "It's not about the helmet, is it? It's about the boys."
Tenzin scowled at the ground. "They call me Bunny Boy."
"I understand. That's unfair." She stayed firm. "But the rule stays: no cycling without a helmet. Your head matters more than their jokes."
Tenzin kicked the tyre. "But—"
"Here's what we can do. Saturday, we'll paint it together. Any colour you want."
Tenzin looked up. "Black? With lightning?"
"Black with lightning. But today, the bunnies go on."
He sighed and buckled it.

qa.q: What was on Tenzin's old helmet?
qa.a: Bunnies.

qa.q: What was Tenzin really feeling behind his defiance?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt by the boys calling him Bunny Boy, so his refusal hid that feeling.

qa.q: How did Tanuja set a firm limit respectfully?
qa.a: She kept the safety rule, explained why, and offered a way to fix the real problem by painting the helmet.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when Tenzin crossed his arms?
qa.a: She might have felt frustrated at first but curious, choosing to ask why instead of just ordering him.

grounding: A child shows defiance about a helmet, which hides embarrassment, and a parent sets a firm, respectful limit with a reason.

passage:
When I was in Class 5, I crossed my arms and said no to going to tuition. Every day at five, I'd hide under the bed or say I had a stomach ache.
My aunt Hansa finally sat me down. "You can't just skip. Tell me why."
I stared at my feet. Then I blurted, "Sir shouts at me when I get it wrong. Everyone laughs."
She didn't scold me. She said, "That sounds scary. But you still need to study." Then she went to the tuition centre the same evening and spoke to Sir. After that, he didn't shout, and she started checking my work at home too.
I still didn't love tuition, but I went.
- Kalyani

qa.q: Where did Kalyani hide at five o'clock?
qa.a: Under the bed.

qa.q: What was Kalyani really feeling when refusing tuition?
qa.a: Kalyani felt scared and embarrassed because of the teacher's shouting and others laughing.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that worked?
qa.a: She listened to the reason behind the defiance, kept the limit about studying, and addressed the unfairness by speaking to the teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might the tuition teacher have seen Kalyani before Hansa spoke to him?
qa.a: He might have thought Kalyani was lazy or careless, not realising his shouting was the cause of the fear.

grounding: The narrator looks back on refusing tuition out of fear, and an adult setting a firm limit while addressing the unfairness.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Wednesday
Irawati refused to sit in her new seat today. She crossed her arms and said, "I won't sit there. It's not fair."
The class watched. I told her calmly, "The seating plan stays for now. Please sit, and we'll talk at break."
She sat, lips pressed tight.
At break she explained: the new seat was right in the sun, and the glare on the board made her eyes water. She couldn't read anything.
I moved her to the other side of the row, away from the window. I explained to the class that seat changes happen for a reason, not as favours.
Irawati didn't smile, but she worked hard all afternoon.
- Usha Ma'am

qa.q: What problem did Irawati have with her new seat?
qa.a: The glare on the board made her eyes water, and she couldn't read anything.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she refused to sit?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and treated unfairly, since the glare made it impossible to see the board.

qa.q: How did Usha Ma'am handle Irawati's defiance?
qa.a: She kept a firm limit by asking her to sit for now, then listened at break and fixed the real problem.

qa.q: How might the class see the seat change?
qa.a: Some might think it was favouritism, but Usha Ma'am's explanation helps them see there was a fair reason.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child's defiance hiding a real unfairness, handled with a firm, respectful limit and a reason.

passage:
Friday
Today at lunch, Shankar opened his tiffin and it was bitter gourd. I said, "Yuck!" and wrinkled my nose. It smelled so strong.
Then Priyanka said, "Shankar smells like bitter gourd," and everyone moved their tiffins away from him. Shankar closed his box and didn't eat.
I felt terrible. My "yuck" started it. It was about the food, not about him. But the others made it about him.
After lunch I told Shankar, "Sorry. I don't like bitter gourd, but you're not yuck." He shrugged but gave a small smile.
Tomorrow I'll sit next to him.
- Ishita

qa.q: What was in Shankar's tiffin?
qa.a: Bitter gourd.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling after the others moved away from Shankar?
qa.a: Ishita felt guilty and sorry, realising the "yuck" about food had turned into excluding Shankar.

qa.q: What did Ishita do to make it right?
qa.a: Ishita apologised to Shankar, explaining the dislike was about the food, not him, and planned to sit next to him.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when everyone moved away?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and embarrassed, left out because of his food.

grounding: A child's diary shows disgust at food turning into exclusion of a person, and choosing kindness instead.

passage:
At the village fair, Saurabh walked past the fish stall and pinched his nose. "Yuck! It stinks!"
Arohi, who was cleaning fish at her family's stall, heard him. She bent her head lower and scrubbed faster.
Saurabh's grandmother, walking with him, stopped. "Saurabh, the smell is strong, yes. But look at her hands. She's working hard to help her family."
Saurabh looked. Arohi's fingers were red from the cold water.
He felt his face go hot. He walked over. "Sorry. The fish smells, but you're not yucky."
Arohi looked up, surprised, and nodded.
On the way home, Saurabh asked his grandmother, "Can we buy fish from her next time?"

qa.q: What did Saurabh do when he passed the fish stall?
qa.a: He pinched his nose and said, "Yuck! It stinks!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she bent her head and scrubbed faster?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt embarrassed and hurt by Saurabh's words.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's grandmother help him?
qa.a: She agreed the smell was strong but pointed out Arohi's hard work, teaching him to separate disgust at smells from how he treats people.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's grandmother see his apology?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and relieved that Saurabh noticed Arohi's hard work and turned a careless yuck into kindness.

grounding: At a village fair, a child's disgust at a smell becomes hurtful to a person, and his grandmother teaches kindness.

passage:
In the school canteen in Oslo, Anders opened his lunchbox and the smell of pickled herring filled the table. Bilal wrinkled his nose. "Eww!"
Others joined in. "Fishy Anders! Fishy Anders!"
Anders shut the box and sat very still.
Bilal suddenly remembered last year, when he brought biryani and someone called it "stinky rice." He remembered how his face burned.
He turned to the others. "Stop. It's just food. I didn't like it, but that doesn't mean we tease him."
Then he said to Anders, "What does it taste like?"
Anders shrugged. "Sour. And a bit sweet."
Bilal took a tiny bite. His face twisted. Anders laughed. "Told you it's sour!"

qa.q: What was in Anders's lunchbox?
qa.a: Pickled herring.

qa.q: Why did Bilal decide to stop the teasing?
qa.a: He remembered feeling embarrassed and hurt when others called his biryani "stinky rice," so he felt empathy for Anders.

qa.q: What did Bilal do that was kind?
qa.a: He told the others to stop, separated disliking food from teasing a person, and showed interest in Anders's food.

qa.q: How might Anders feel after Bilal tasted the herring?
qa.a: Anders probably felt relieved and included, laughing together instead of being teased.

grounding: In a school canteen, a child's disgust at food nearly becomes exclusion, and he chooses kindness.

passage:
"Didi, at the cycle stand today, that big boy Vikas glared at me. His fists were tight, and he shouted, 'Move your cycle, or else!'"
Vandana put down her book. "Santosh, what did you do?"
"I just stood there. I didn't know what to do."
"Did he touch you?"
"No. But his face was red and angry."
Vandana nodded. "Those are signs he might hurt you. Next time, walk away and go where there are other people. Don't argue."
"But he'll think I'm scared."
"Better he thinks that than you get hurt. And you should tell a teacher. Let's tell Papa now."
They found Papa in the kitchen. He listened, then said, "I'll call the class teacher tonight, and I'll walk you to the cycle stand tomorrow." Santosh let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Vikas shout at Santosh?
qa.a: "Move your cycle, or else!"

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he stood still at the cycle stand?
qa.a: Santosh felt scared and unsure, not knowing what to do when Vikas glared and shouted.

qa.q: What steps did Vandana and Papa take to keep Santosh safe?
qa.a: Vandana taught him to move away and stay with others, then took him to Papa, who listened, planned to call the teacher that night and walk him to the stand.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt hearing about Vikas?
qa.a: Vandana probably felt worried and protective, wanting her brother to stay safe and get help quickly.

grounding: A child learns to spot signs of possible danger like glaring and tight fists, and the safe reaction is to move away and tell a trusted adult.

passage:
On the playground in Class 4, I saw an older girl yelling at Nazia near the swings. Her face was red, and her fists were tight. Nazia looked frozen.
My stomach flipped. I remembered what our teacher had said about signs of danger: glaring, shouting, fists.
I ran to Nazia, grabbed her hand, and said, "Come, the others are calling us." We went to the group of friends near the tap.
Then I told Ma'am on duty straight away. Ma'am went to talk to the older girl, and later called Nazia and me to her room to check we were okay. She said we did the right thing.
I felt shaky all day, but proud.
- Ganga

qa.q: Where did Ganga and Nazia go after leaving the swings?
qa.a: To the group of friends near the tap.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on seeing the older girl yelling?
qa.a: Ganga felt scared and uneasy, recognising the red face and tight fists as signs of danger.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that was safe and wise?
qa.a: Ganga moved Nazia away to a group of friends and told the teacher on duty straight away.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt when Ganga grabbed her hand?
qa.a: Nazia probably felt relieved and safer, no longer alone with the angry girl.

grounding: The narrator recalls spotting signs of possible danger in a bully and choosing to move away, stay with others, and tell an adult.

Teacher's note, Thursday
At the drinking tap today, Tarun noticed a Class 7 boy shouting at a younger boy, fists clenched, face red. Tarun didn't join in or argue. He walked to the group of children near the bench and then came straight to me.
"Sir, that boy looks like he'll hit someone," he said quickly.
I went at once. The older boy stopped shouting when I arrived. I sent the younger boy to class with a friend and spoke to the older boy in my room.
Later I called Tarun and told him he did the right thing: moving away, staying with others, and telling an adult.
I will inform both families this evening.
- Ujjwal Sir
